body:
Childhood & Early Life

Katherine Fowler was born in London on New Year's Day, 1632, the daughter of John Fowler, a prosperous cloth merchant. She was a bookish, precocious kid who, by the account of a friend, could recite long chunks of scripture and loved reading from a very early age. Her father died in 1642, just as England slid into civil war, and her mother soon remarried a Welshman, Hector Philipps, who took the family to Wales.

Before that she went to a boarding school in Hackney run by a Mrs Salmon, and this is where the real story begins. She met Mary Aubrey there, and the two girls became so devoted that Katherine kept writing to her for years. Later she would give Mary a nickname, Rosania. The habit of renaming her friends would define her life.

What She Did & Why She's Remembered

Katherine Philips, who called herself Orinda, was among the first English women to be famous as a poet in her own lifetime. She wrote about friendship between women with an intensity most people reserved for love, and she did it in a world that gave women almost no public voice. She also translated Corneille's play Pompey, which was staged in Dublin in 1663 and then in London, making her one of the first women to have a play produced in English. Poets after her, Dryden among them, treated her as proof that a woman could be a serious writer.

Family Life

At sixteen she married James Philips, a Welsh Parliamentarian roughly thirty years older, and moved to the Priory in Cardigan. The marriage seems to have been steady rather than passionate; he supported her writing and she wrote about him with respect. They lost a baby son, Hector, in infancy in 1655, and she wrote an elegy for him, "Epitaph on Hector Philips," that is still hard to read. A daughter, Katherine, survived.

Politics was a danger in her home. Her family and friends were Royalists while her husband sat on the other side, and when the monarchy returned in 1660 James was suddenly in trouble. Katherine used her contacts to help protect him, and part of her ambition was practical: she needed the right people to like her.

Romantic Life

There is no record of a love affair in the usual sense, and I'm not going to invent one. What there is, is the Society of Friendship, a circle she built in Wales where everyone took a classical pen name. Rosania was Mary Aubrey, Lucasia was Anne Owen, and Poliarchus was Sir Charles Cotterell, who became her literary go-between in London. She was Orinda, and her poems to Lucasia are some of the most passionate of the century: they talk about souls merging, hearts as altars, and a love that rejects the world's disapproval. Whether that was romance, devotion or a mix, she was writing about it openly.

It also cost her. When Anne Owen married Marcus Trevor in 1662 and left for Ireland, Katherine was devastated, and the poems turn harsh. Friendship, it turned out, did not shield her from heartbreak.

Life Until Death

In 1662 she traveled to Dublin, partly to see Lucasia and partly to push her translation of Pompey into production. It was a triumph. A year later, an unauthorised edition of her poems appeared in London, which mortified her; a woman of her standing was not supposed to publish, and she wrote that she was horrified that her private verses were out. She took her time denying she had approved it.

In June 1664 she caught smallpox in London and died on the 22nd, aged thirty-two. Her authorised collected poems came out in 1667, and the book's title page called her "the matchless Orinda."

Her Works

Her best-known poem, written to Lucasia, is the one that sounds like it could have been written yesterday. Spelling is from the 1667 edition.

Friendship's Mystery, To my Dearest Lucasia

Come, my Lucasia, since we see
That Miracles Mens faith do move,
By wonder and by prodigy
To the dull angry world let's prove
There's a Religion in our Love.
For though we were design'd t' agree,
That Fate no liberty destroyes,
But our Election is as free
As Angels, who with greedy choice
Are yet determin'd to their joyes.
Our hearts are doubled by the loss,
Here Mixture is Addition grown;
We both diffuse, and both ingross:
And we whose minds are so much one,
Never, yet ever are alone.
We court our own Captivity
Than Thrones more great and innocent:
'Twere banishment to be set free,
Since we wear fetters whose intent
Not Bondage is, but Ornament.
Divided joyes are tedious found,
And griefs united easier grow:
We are our selves but by rebound,
And all our Titles shuffled so,
Both Princes, and both Subjects too.
Our Hearts are mutual Victims laid,
While they (such power in Friendship lies)
Are Altars, Priests, and Off'rings made:
And each Heart which thus kindly dies,
Grows deathless by the Sacrifice.

To my Excellent Lucasia, on our Friendship

I did not live until this time
Crowned my felicity,
When I could say without a crime,
I am not thine, but thee.
This carcass breathed, and walked, and slept,
So that the world believed
There was a soul the motions kept;
But they were all deceived.
For as a watch by art is wound
To motion, such was mine:
But never had Orinda found
A soul till she found thine;
Which now inspires, cures and supplies,
And guides my darkened breast:
For thou art all that I can prize,
My joy, my life, my rest.
No bridegroom's nor crown-conqueror's mirth
To mine compared can be:
They have but pieces of the earth,
I've all the world in thee.
Then let our flames still light and shine,
And no false fear control,
As innocent as our design,
Immortal as our soul.

Texts from the 1667 Poems (via Representative Poetry Online) and the Poetry Foundation.
epi: The Matchless Orinda, who wrote about friendship as a religion
